summary: Josef Maria Abs worked in Indology and philosophy, studying under Hermann Jacobi at the University of Bonn (~1913–1921). He held a professorship at the University of Calcutta in 1914.

A scholar of Iranian and Central Asian studies, history, archaeology, and linguistics, Markwart earned his Ph.D. at Tübingen (~1889–1893) and studied at Bonn. He worked at the National Museum of Ethnology (1900–1912) and Berlin (1912).

A scholar in history, archaeology, and other fields, Partsch studied at the University of Breslau (~1901–1905). He held posts at Berlin (~1906–1908), Geneva (~1912–1914), Göttingen (~1914–1917), Freiburg (~1917–1920), and Bonn (~1920–1922).

A linguist, Schick studied under Albrecht Weber (~1880–1882) and at Tübingen and Berlin (Ph.D. 1887–1889). He held posts at Berlin, Bonn, and Heidelberg before serving as ordentlicher Professor at Munich (1896–1925).

A specialist in art history and archaeology, Strzygowski studied at Vienna, Berlin, and Munich (Ph.D. ~1884–1885). He held posts at Graz, Åbo Akademi University, and Vienna, where he served as Professor of Art History (1909–1933).

A scholar of Indology and linguistics, Zubatý studied under Alfred Ludwig at Charles University (~1876–1883, Ph.D.). He spent his career at Charles University, serving as Professor of Sanskrit and comparative Indo-European from 1894 to 1925.
Josef van Ess was a scholar of religious studies and other fields who studied at the University of Bonn (~1954–1959). He held a post at the University of Tübingen from ~1968 to 1999.
Joseph Ammann was an Indology scholar who studied under Othmar Frank. In 1836, he served as a teacher at Hans-Carossa-Gymnasium Landshut.

Campbell studied at Dartmouth, Columbia, Paris, and Munich. A scholar in religious studies, he held early posts at Columbia and Canterbury School before teaching at Sarah Lawrence College from 1934 to 1972.
Joseph D. Markowski is a scholar of Buddhist studies and Japanology who completed a Master of Arts degree at McGill University under the supervision of G. Victor Sōgen Hori (attested 2004).

An Indologist and religious studies scholar, Dahlmann studied under Georg Bühler in Vienna and completed a Ph.D. at Berlin. He co-founded and taught at Sophia University (1913) and taught at the University of Tokyo (1914–1924).

Hooker earned an M.D. from the University of Glasgow (~1832–1839). He worked at the British Geological Survey (1845–1847) and served as Assistant Director and Director at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew (1855–1885).

Trained in civil engineering at Shibpur, Beglar worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. He served in the Bengal Public Works Department and the Archaeological Survey of India, becoming Archaeological Surveyor of Bengal (1885–1890).

A scholar of Indology and history, Schwartzberg completed his Ph.D. under Richard Hartshorne at Wisconsin (1956–1960). He held posts at the University of Pennsylvania, JNU, and the University of Minnesota (1964–2000).

Harry studied at Johns Hopkins under Maurice Bloomfield. He held posts as Professor of Greek and German at Georgetown College (1888–1900), Professor of Greek at Cincinnati (1900–1916), and taught at the Sorbonne and Bard College.
A scholar of linguistics and Indology, Brandreth was educated at Eton College and East India Company College. He served as a Member of the Imperial Legislative Council from 1867 to 1869.

A scholar of Buddhist studies, Indology, and religion, Carpenter studied at UCL, Harris Manchester College, and Zurich. He served as professor, president, and principal at Harris Manchester College, and later Wilde Lecturer at Oxford (1914–1924).
Joseph Gabet was a scholar of Tibetology, Sinology, and religious studies. He studied at the Petit Séminaire de Vaux-sur-Poligny (~1823–1828) and the Grand Séminaire de Saint-Claude (~1828–1833).

Goldstein studied at Columbia University and under numerous Buddhist teachers, including Anagarika Munindra and Satya Narayan Goenka. Working in Buddhist and religious studies, he taught at Naropa University in 1974.

Hackin studied in Paris under Sylvain Lévi, Louis Finot, Édouard Chavannes, and Paul Pelliot. Working in archaeology and Buddhist studies, he served at the Guimet Museum (1913–1941) and directed the Délégation Archéologique Française en Afghanistan (1934).
